citations.quote: Andreas Freimann University of Würzburg, Germany, freimann@informatik.uni-wuerzburg.de

It is shown that energy simulations can improve the mission design and the operation of satellites, e.g. by proper load distribution between the nodes in a satellite formation. The satellite formation NetSat is used as an example to compare both approaches.
In this paper, an energy simulation approach is presented that allows system engineers and operators to analyze the available energy of satellites more accurately and in a timely manner.

We model and simulate the dynamic power generation and consumption of a system which allows us to identify if the satellite runs out of energy in specific situations and if consumption exceeds a maximum current. This model is implemented in ESTNeT[1], an OMNeT++ based simulation framework for space-terrestrial networks.

In section 2 the model of the generation of energy by solar panels is presented before in section 3 the model for the power consumption by different satellite subsystems is described. The power budget approach described in section 4 and the simulation approach, described in section 5, are compared to each other in section 6.

The generated power mainly depends on the illumination angle and the size of the area of solar panels illuminated by the sun, therefore the power that will be available during the course of a mission can not simply be calculated in advance.
The EPS stores energy that is usually generated by solar cells and supplies all subsystems of the satellite with energy.

Most subsystems have a finite number of modes that is traversed, the simplest of them being the on and off states. By defining power consumption values and proportional durations for each mode the overall consumption of a subsystem can be calculated. Finally the overall consumption of a CubeSat can be defined by combining different subsystems.

Furthermore the activity of subsystems can be coupled to the status of another subsystem. For example the ADCS, which is active if the camera or the propulsion system is active to orient the satellite appropriately. Activities can also be defined beforehand and executed by a schedule which is uploaded to the satellite, such as sensor measurements.

The consumption of the COMM and the ACS can be simulated in ESTNeT based on their actual status. The activity of a satellite transceiver is simulated based on the actual network traffic. The COMM switches its states accordingly during the simulation and records the respective power consumption.
The power calculation assumes a linear correlation between power consumption and angular acceleration. At maximum torque the ACS consumes a power of $ P_{max} $ .
In the worst case scenario for energy generation, the angle $ \beta $ is assumed to be 0.
The resulting mean power generated per orbit is $ P_{gen}=5.5W. $
The result in this case is, that the satellite will produce more energy than it consumes as $ P_{gen}>P_{cons} $ . Thus, the power supply of the satellite is assumed to be sufficient.
Additionally to the typical power budget calculations presented in section 4 a comprehensive model has been implemented.

Figure 1 shows the structure of the energy module with its submodules. The solar panel module calculates the amount of generated energy based on the model presented in section 2. The battery module calculates the state of charge taking into account the maximum capacity and the system efficiency.
If multiple consumer types are defined for a single consumer the module always considers the highest consumption value of consumer types.
For comparison simulations based on the parameters of the NetSat[2] mission have been performed. This mission consists of four 3U CubeSats, as shown in figure 2.
Table 4 shows the configuration of the simulation regarding subsystem models, consumption types and subsystem modes.

The activity of the OCS was simulated in a different simulator based on Orekit. The model predictive controller presented in [3] controls the orbit maneuvers to keep the formation. The resulting thrust vectors are imported into ESTNeT to simulate the power consumption of the OCS and the required attitude maneuvers by the ACS.
The resulting State of Charge (SoC) of the satellite batteries show that one of the satellites runs out of energy multiple times during the simulation period of 7 days, see figure 3.

In this example one satellite is undersupplied due to a worse orientation of its solar panels. The reason for that is the orientation defined by the formation control algorithm to point the thrusters appropriately. The power generation decreases during orbit maneuvers as shown in figure 4(a). Together with the consumption of the thrusters this leads to temporary power supply problems that have not been recognized using simple power budgets.

Based on the relation of the activity of the OCS and the power generation a potential improvement is to perform orbit maneuvers when the satellites is in eclipse, as shown in figure 4(b). This leads to increased power generation since the solar panels can be pointed towards the sun when the satellite is illuminated by the sun instead of pointing the thrusters.

Generally, by simulations of the SoC of satellites the usage of all satellite subsystems can be adjusted to improve the load balancing of the satellites and prevent power outages by planning subsystem activities accordingly. Furthermore the overall activity schedule of all satellite subsystems can be optimized to prevent that too many consumers are active simultaneously, resulting in exceeding the load limit of the EPS.
The evaluations show that the simulation allows system engineers and satellite operators to perform better analyses and thereby increase the outcome of satellite missions.

Improving orbit control and network communication algorithms for better load balancing in multi-satellite systems and avoiding power outages preventatively by appropriate software concepts are left as further work.
The orientation of directional antennas also leaves one degree of freedom that can be used to maximize the power consumption.
It is obvious that this approach includes a lot of estimations and simplifications.

Usually it is estimated for which percentage of an orbital period the subsystems are expected to be active or these values are derived from reference systems. The mean durations and the standard deviations can be defined to characterize the duty cycle of such systems.
